notes.short: The tenants who killed the owner's son
notes.about: Jesus tells of tenants who beat and kill the owner's servants, then kill his son to take his inheritance. His hearers pass sentence on such tenants in verse 41, and verse 45 says the leaders knew He was speaking about them. Many read the servants as the prophets and the son as Jesus Himself.

figure.name: Parable
figure.words: he rented it out to some tenants
figure.means: the leaders of Israel, given charge of God's people, who mistreated the prophets He sent and would kill His Son; verse 45 says they knew He meant them

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry: the Jewish nation and its leaders are the tenants, the servants the prophets. John Calvin: the rulers would rob God, as with the prophets, and slay His Son. Albert Barnes: the Son is Jesus Christ, sent after the prophets. David Brown (JFB): the tenants are the people's guides. Chrysostom (Thomas Aquinas' Catena Aurea): it was told so they would judge themselves.
notes.limit: Not every detail is pressed: the note claims the parable's main drift, which the hearers saw, not a meaning for each wall, winepress or tower.

notes.short: Not willing to come: a flat refusal from the heart
notes.about: The king's guests refused to come. Matthew's Greek says, more mildly, that they were not willing to come. The mild words make the refusal stronger: they refused outright, and did so by their own wish.

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.words: they refused to come
figure.means: an outright refusal made by their own wish, told in Matthew's Greek in the milder words not willing

original.note: In Matthew's Greek the words are ouk ēthelon elthein, they were not willing to come.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis: Matthew's Greek says they did not wish to come, and so stresses that they refused outright and acted on the wish of their own hearts.
notes.limit: The English here already gives the stronger sense, refused; the milder wording is in Matthew's Greek.

cites.quote: The Greek is:- οὐκ ἤθελον ἐλθεῖν (ouk eethelon elthein), they did not wish to come, this is enhancing, by Meiosis, the fact that they not only absolutely refused, but in doing so they acted only on the wish of their heart.

notes.short: A saying: where the carcass is, vultures gather
notes.about: Jesus uses a saying that echoes Job 39:30: wherever a carcass lies, vultures gather. As the birds surely find a dead body, judgment will surely come wherever a people is lifeless and corrupt. Some of the writers apply it first to Jerusalem's fall to the armies of Rome.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather
figure.means: as vultures find a dead body, God's judgment will surely come wherever a people is lifeless and corrupt

notes.evidence: Bullinger (Figures of Speech) lists it under Parœmia, says it is from Job 39:30 and reads it with Luke 17:37 of a time of judgment. Barnes calls the words proverbial, applies them to Rome's armies and Jerusalem, and finds in them a universal truth; Benson says our Lord applies a proverbial expression to the Romans; Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) calls it a proverb of judgment where life is gone.
notes.limit: The writers agree it is a saying but differ on how far it reaches: some apply it chiefly to Rome's armies coming on Jerusalem, others to a law of judgment seen again and again until the end.
